P3-MESH-HORIZON-SENTENCE: One difference between the mesh and the link budget has to be stated. The mesh keeps pairs of 1.0 m antennas up to 5 km apart wherever the terrain shows line of sight, although the smooth-Moon horizon of two such antennas is 3.73 km. Both are right: the ridge is not a sphere, and two antennas on two rises see each other across a valley farther than a sphere allows, while two on a plain do not. The horizon check is therefore off on the terrain mesh and on in Table 7; switched on in the mesh it would remove 6.9 % of the links between 1.0 m antennas and none between rover antennas. Under the two-ray law every link of the mesh closes 16 kbit/s at margins of 3 and 10 dB for every class; at 15 dB 94.2 % of the small rover's links and 99.1 % of the hopper's do, and in the month's trace of Section 4.2 no link in use is lost either way (Assumed on paths the terrain shows as visible: no path loss has been measured on the Moon).

The second is a mean over positions at decision epochs, and in the recorded month a vehicle is parked in 97 % of its steps. P3-E48-LINK-LAW-SENTENCE: The hop is 5 km long, between two antennas of the class's own height (for the base computer, the mast down to a 1.0 m robot antenna). Its loss follows the flat-ground two-ray law: free-space loss up to the breakpoint 4h<sub>1</sub>h<sub>2</sub>/λ and, beyond it, 40 log<sub>10</sub> d − 20 log<sub>10</sub>(h<sub>1</sub>h<sub>2</sub>) with the distance d and the antenna heights h<sub>1</sub>, h<sub>2</sub> in metres, never less than free-space loss and independent of frequency (Derived from a direct ray and a ground-reflected ray with a reflection coefficient of −1 at grazing incidence; a NASA Johnson Space Center model of lunar surface propagation shows the same fourth-power law and its independence of frequency at long range [21]). A hop longer than the smooth-Moon horizon of its two antennas, √(2Rh<sub>1</sub>) + √(2Rh<sub>2</sub>) [63], carries nothing; for a class in that case the rate is reported at the longest hop the horizon allows. The rate is the Shannon capacity of a 1 MHz channel with 3 dBi antennas, a 5 dB noise figure and a 10 dB margin (Assumed). The rate under free-space loss at the same hop is kept beside it as an upper bound.

Third, with terrain fixes the percentile stays inside the budget away from the base, that is, where fewer than two beacons are in line of sight: not supported (15.2 m [14.5, 16.0] at today's fleet, 12.2 m [11.6, 12.9] at four times the fleet, 11.5 m [10.7, 12.1] at eight times the fleet); with fixes the percentile at today's fleet is 4.76 m where one or more beacons are in view (23 of 30 seeds inside), 9.12 m within 1 km and 12.6 m over all driving. With the navigation service as assumed for 2030 the value away from the base is 7.54 m [7.09, 8.00] at today's fleet, 6.76 m [6.38, 7.09] at four times the fleet, 6.44 m [5.98, 6.86] at eight times the fleet, still outside the budget.
P3-E50-FIXSTOP-SENTENCE: Terrain fixes cost standing time, 120 s each: 37.3 h [35.5, 39.1] a month for the eight vehicles of today's fleet and 168.7 h [163.7, 174.0] a month for the 32 vehicles of four times the fleet and 354.4 h [331.2, 371.7] a month for the 64 vehicles of eight times the fleet. E50 replays recorded trajectories and does not move the vehicles, so the delay it reports for the widened margins, which the companion paper quotes [61], does not include those stops; a dated change of [67] labels it “without stop time”.
P3-E50-8X-SENTENCE: At eight times the fleet the same percentiles were dead reckoning alone 905.5 m [826.5, 984.5]; with ranging 31.3 m [29.8, 33.1]; with ranging and terrain fixes 10.1 m [9.4, 10.7]; with the navigation service as assumed for 2030 5.6 m [5.3, 6.0].
P3-E50B-SENTENCE: A follow-up run, E50b, put the stops into the engine; it was registered after E50's first results and run after them, so it is exploratory [67]. At today's fleet, on the same 30 seeds, whose arm without stop time reproduces E50's cells exactly, the delay per delivery rose from 17.74 h without stop time to 18.37 h with it, by 0.63 h [0.02, 1.29] or 3.5 %; the bootstrap interval excludes zero, a paired t-test gives p = 0.066, and the delay was higher in 22 seeds and lower in 8. The time spent waiting at roads did not change (−0.07 h [−0.31, 0.11]), and no run with stop time had a violation. This is the price of the terrain-fix layer in delay, and it is a lower bound: the engine inserted 26.6 h of stops a month, 71 % of the 37.3 h of fix time in the navigation replay, because the other stops fall on repositioning drives, which do not pass through the road layer; a stop that falls inside a single-lane segment (25 % of the fixes) is taken just after the segment's exit.
P3-TIME-SCALE-SENTENCE: Proposition 3 derives the offset term by term and gives 56.02 µs a day, a rate of 6.4844 × 10<sup>−10</sup>, which is the constant the clock model of E51 uses; left uncorrected it is 16.8 km of light time a day, and without the Moon's own potential it would be 58.7 µs a day.
P3-TIME-MODEL-SENTENCE: The model has two classes. A temperature-compensated crystal has a constant frequency error drawn per vehicle, uniformly between 0 and 8 × 10<sup>−7</sup> and so of one sign. That range is the excursion the crystal of one receiver, LuGRE's, showed on the lunar surface as it warmed from 25 to 45 °C [82] (read from a figure's axis); using one crystal's excursion as the spread of constant offsets across vehicles is our modelling choice (Assumed). A chip-scale atomic clock has a frequency error with a standard deviation of 3 × 10<sup>−10</sup>, its temperature term, and ages by 9 × 10<sup>−10</sup> a month [86] (Spec; the data sheet says the model is not rated for space). A vehicle is synchronised by a two-way time transfer whenever it has a radio path to the base mast, which leaves a residual of 100 ns (Assumed) and corrects the offset, not the frequency (Assumed; Section 5.9 reports a variant that steers frequency). A reservation is stamped in the vehicle's own clock and keeps a guard of 0.1 s (Assumed).
P3-E51-DESIGN-SENTENCE: E51 replays the month of E50 at today's fleet, the perfect-position run of each of 30 seeds, and gives every vehicle a clock of one class. Resynchronisation is attempted every 10 s, 1 min, 10 min, 1 h, 6 h or 1 day, or never, and succeeds only when the vehicle has a radio path to the base mast over the mesh; 6.8 % of the attempts find none. The measures are the error a clock adds to one-way ranging against a beacon on the base's clock (the speed of light times the clock error), to single-sided two-way ranging between two vehicles with a reply delay of 1 ms, and to a time-stamped position at 1 m/s; the largest clock error; and the reservation conflicts caused by clock error alone. Such a conflict is a pair of conflicting single-lane reservations, of 303 such pairs in the 30 seeds, whose two clock errors close the nominal gap between them by more than twice the guard; the guard is 0.1 s, with a row for no guard. This is a check on the logged reservations, not a new run of the engine, and it is made at today's fleet only: the fleets of four and eight times, where reservations are more frequent, were not checked. Four things were added after the first results and are labelled post hoc (Section 4.6): guards of 0.01 and 1 s; every vehicle on Earth seconds; a transfer that also steers frequency, with a daily thermal cycle of 4 × 10<sup>−7</sup> on the crystal and 3 × 10<sup>−10</sup> on the atomic clock (Assumed period of 24 h); and a mixed fleet in which half the vehicles count Earth seconds, with and without the conversion of Proposition 3.
P3-E51-RESULTS-SENTENCE: With the crystal, the error added to one-way ranging at the 95th percentile was 975 km at a resync interval of 10 s, 1,790 km at a resync interval of 1 h, 29,500 km at a resync interval of 1 day, and 345,000 km never resynchronised; the largest clock error ran from 328 ms to 2.1 s, the error of a position stamp at 1 m/s from 4.3 mm to 790 mm, and single-sided two-way ranging between vehicles 84 mm at every interval. With the atomic clock, the error added to one-way ranging at the 95th percentile was 1.61 km at a resync interval of 10 s, 3.23 km at a resync interval of 1 h, 42.4 km at a resync interval of 1 day, and 460 km never resynchronised; the largest clock error ran from 0.60 ms to 3.6 ms, the error of a position stamp at 1 m/s from 0.0090 mm to 1.9 mm, and single-sided two-way ranging between vehicles 0.11 mm at every interval. With perfect clocks every measure is zero, the baseline. The crystal's 95th percentile is set by vehicles that are out of contact and free-run however often a transfer is attempted, vehicles that could not range to the base either: at a 10 s resync its median is 92 m and its largest clock error 328 ms (Table 11). Two-way ranging, which Section 3.5 uses, is unaffected by the interval because the clock offset cancels in it.
P3-E51-GUARD-SENTENCE: Counted over the 30 seeds, and with the 0.01 and 1 s guards added post hoc, the crystal caused no clock-only reservation conflict with a guard of 1 s even when it is never resynchronised, with a guard of 0.1 s with a resync at least every 6 h (1 at the next longer interval, 15 never resynchronised), and with a guard of 0.01 s with a resync at least every 1 h (2 at the next longer interval, 24 never resynchronised); with no guard it caused 1 to 26 at every interval. Its largest clock error when never resynchronised was 2.1 s. The atomic clock caused none with any guard at any interval, and 22 to 25 with none. The column without a guard needs care: it counts a pair as soon as the two clock errors close the nominal gap at all, and for reservations booked back to back, with no nominal gap, that is the sign of the difference of two clock errors, however small. It is a count of back-to-back pairs and not of conflicts a vehicle would meet, which is why the better clock shows more of them than the crystal at a 10 s resync.
P3-H11-VERDICT-SENTENCE: H11 of [67] asks for a resync interval at which the cheaper oscillator causes no reservation conflict while its clock error still adds more to one-way ranging than the ranging radio's own noise of 0.3 m. The first half was observed: with the 0.1 s guard every interval from 10 s to 6 h gave no clock-caused conflict in any seed, over the 303 pairs of conflicting single-lane reservations in the recorded months. The second half is not a test. The time transfer is assumed to leave 100 ns, which is 30 m of range, so the clock error exceeds the radio's noise for any oscillator, a perfect one included: it is a design calculation on that assumed residual and could not have come out otherwise (a dated entry of [67]). By the registered rule the hypothesis counts as supported; it is exploratory and outside the confirmatory family.
P3-E51B-STEERING-SENTENCE: With a daily thermal cycle on the frequency and a transfer that also estimates it (post hoc), steering cut the crystal's one-way ranging error at the 95th percentile by a factor of 1.5 to 7.1; steering cut the atomic clock's one-way ranging error at the 95th percentile by a factor of 2.6 to 7.3 at resync intervals of 10 min and longer and made it worse at 1 min, 5.19 km against 1.63 km, because the estimate's own noise there, 2.4 × 10<sup>−9</sup>, is larger than the clock's frequency error. No steering cell had a clock-caused conflict with the 0.1 s guard.
P3-E51B-MIXED-SENTENCE: In a fleet where half the vehicles count Earth seconds (post hoc), one-way ranging between two vehicles on different scales was 18 % to 24 % worse for the atomic clock without the conversion of Proposition 3 than with it (42.7 km against 34.5 km at a resync interval of 10 min), and less than 0.1 % worse for the crystal, whose own drift hides the offset. The count of clock-caused reservation conflicts between vehicles on different scales was the same with and without the conversion at every interval and guard, and zero for the atomic clock.
P3-MAP-FRAME-SENTENCE: Proposition 5 gives the size of the mistake the identifier prevents: the same numbers read in the other frame move a point by 662.9 m at the south pole, 659.2 m at the centre of our terrain tile and 875.2 m at most, computed from the three angles of the NAIF frame kernel [88] and equal to a direct evaluation with the SPICE toolkit to within 0.05 m [68].
P3-MAP-SYNC-SENTENCE: On the wire a 256 m tile of 1 m cells weighs 2,048 B as a hazard layer, at 0.25 bit a cell (Assumed; a slope mask of our own terrain compressed to a median of 0.12 bit a cell), 11,796 B as a traversability layer, at the 1.44 bits a cell that five slope classes of our terrain compressed to, and 32,768 B as rover-made elevation, at 4 bits a cell (Assumed). These are computed from tile sizes, not from a flown map [68]. The 16 km site has 3,969 such tiles a layer. With 42 of them changed in a day (Assumed: half the tiles the haul routes cross), the hash-tree walk costs at most 8,072 B a layer by Proposition 6, against 39,690 B for a flat list of every tile's version and hash; the tree is the smaller for up to 206 changed tiles (the bound is n below 206.7). Both counts are hash bytes in one direction, without the replies that say which children differ and without message headers. The tiles themselves then come to 86.0 kB of hazards, which go first, and 1.96 MB for the three layers together.
P3-E52-DESIGN-SENTENCE: E52 keeps the base's map and one rover's copy of it for the 16 km site: 3,969 tiles of 256 m in each of the hazard, traversability and rover-made elevation layers and a radio-coverage layer in 1,280 m tiles of 2,000 B, at the wire sizes of Section 3.7. The rover loops the haul routes at 1 m/s; the routes cross 60 tiles. While it is out of contact, 42 route tiles a day get a new version in each of the three layers, and new hazards appear on the routes at 2 a day, keep-out zones at 0.3 a day and road-edge changes at 5 a day; 50 % of the hazards are invisible to the rover's own sensors (all Assumed). After 1 h, 6 h, 1, 3, 7 or 14 days the rover regains a link of 10, 16, 100 or 1,000 kbit/s with a packet loss of 0.2 and synchronises, either hazards first (keep-out zones, hazard tiles on its route, other hazards, roads, traversability, radio coverage, elevation) or oldest change first, over 30 seeds. The outcomes are the bytes sent against a full resend of every raster layer (185.5 MB), the time until the hazard layer is current, and the hazards the rover drives into because its copy is stale, during the outage and after contact.
P3-E52-RESULTS-SENTENCE: After a day out of contact the rover's copy was behind by 126 tile versions on average. Bringing it up to date took 1.97 MB, 1.06 % of a full resend, of which the hash-tree walk was 4,351 B, against 120,760 B for a flat list of every tile. At 16 kbit/s the hazard layer was current after 57.6 s with hazards first and after 20.1 min with the oldest change first, 21 times later; everything was current after 20.5 min in either order. The bytes level off: 78 kB after an hour, 489 kB after six hours, 2.74 MB after three days and 2.81 MB after fourteen, when every route tile has changed in each of the three layers. The hazards the rover drove into because its copy was stale were, during the outage itself, 0.02 for an hour out of contact, 0.80 for a day and 13.8 for fourteen days, and after contact at most 0.08 with hazards first and 1.65 with the oldest change first, at any outage and link rate (means over 30 seeds; Table 13).
P3-H12-VERDICT-SENTENCE: H12 of [67] was registered as a hypothesis with two clauses for a rover that was out of contact for 24 h. Neither is a test: both are design calculations on the assumed inputs and could not have failed, and a dated entry of [67] records it. First, that a hazards-first sync of changed tiles needs under 10 % of the bytes of a full resend: with 42 route tiles assumed to change a day in each of three layers of 3,969 tiles, the changed tiles are 126 of 11,907, 1.06 % of the map, so a sync of changed tiles is 1.06 % of a full resend; the result is the assumption. Second, that it brings the hazard layer current sooner than oldest-first at every link rate: a subset sent first is always finished first, in every seed, and the paired means, 30.6 min at 10 kbit/s, 19.1 min at 16 kbit/s, 3.1 min at 100 kbit/s, 18.3 s at 1,000 kbit/s, are in exact inverse ratio to the link rate. What E52 adds to the arithmetic is the sizes of Table 13 and the count of stale-map hits.
P3-E52-LIMIT-CLAUSE: a rover out of contact for a day drove into 0.8 hazards its copy did not show, and one out for fourteen days into 13.8, all during the outage; after contact the count was at most 1.6 in any cell
P3-SEC-LAYOUT-SENTENCE: The messages are implemented and serialised, unlike the assumed layouts of Section 3.4: 15 message types in one schema with two encodings, bit-packed for the narrow channel and CBOR for the broadband one, with real AES-CMAC and Ed25519 and 45 conformance vectors per version in the repository; the vectors test the codec, not a radio. There are two versions, and what each puts on the wire has to be said exactly. In both, a position report holds east and north in the site grid (24 bits at 0.01 m each), the height above the site datum (16 bits at 0.1 m), heading (12 bits), speed (10 bits), one scalar one-sigma horizontal uncertainty (8 bits at 0.05 m), a 3-bit code for the navigation source and a moving flag, and the 8-byte protocol header adds the version, the message type, the sender and one time stamp in tenths of a second. Version 0.1, with which the experiments of this paper were first run, stops there: 6 bits of the report are spare, and nothing in any message names the frame, the datum or the time scale. Version 0.2 closes that gap in two ways. The uncertainty travels in the report itself: the 6 bits that were spare carry a 95 % horizontal bound on a logarithmic scale, 0.05 m times 2 to the power of a quarter of the code, rounded upward so that the decoded bound never understates, with one code for a bound above 1.95 km and one for unknown. The frame, the datum and the time scale do not travel in every report: each sender declares them, in 6, 6 and 4 bits, in a heartbeat sent at least every 10 s and in its signed manifest, and the declaration is bound to the security context: it holds for the key epoch under which it was authenticated, and a receiver refuses a position report whose sender has no declaration under its current key epoch, as it refuses an unauthenticated one. A covariance is not carried in either version: the report has a one-sigma value and, in version 0.2, a 95 % bound, both scalars. The report is 104 bits, 13 B, in both versions: 27 B with its packet and protocol headers, 41 B with the security header and the 8-byte code, and 49 B with the 16-byte code; these are packet sizes before link framing and coding, and a Proximity-1 frame adds 12 B [94]. A status report is 43 B, a bid 37 B, a reservation request 35 B, and the signed award and grant 92 and 94 B. Two sizes differ between the versions: the heartbeat, 30 B in version 0.1 and 32 B with the declaration, and the capability manifest of the small rover, 283 and 292 B in compact binary (1,200 and 1,235 B as JSON). The identifiers are the site's own registry (Assumed; not registered with any agency). The traffic model of Section 4.2 sends 11 of the 15 types: the three reports, the alert, the bid, the award and the task state, the three reservation messages and the heartbeat; the task announcement, the capability query and manifest and the map notice are not in it.
P3-LIMIT-LRIP-SENTENCE: The design of Sections 3.5 to 3.7 asked for a frame, a datum, a time scale and a covariance with every position. Version 0.2 gives the first three by a declaration per sender, bound to its key epoch, not by fields in each report, and it gives a scalar 95 % bound where the design asked for a covariance; a receiver that needs the shape of the error does not get it. The identifiers are the site's own registry and are registered nowhere. The experiments were run with version 0.1; the figures of version 0.2 are a calculation on the same traffic model, which sends 11 of the 15 message types, and they are packet sizes: a Proximity-1 frame adds 12 B a packet and coding more. The 45 conformance vectors of each version test the codec against itself; no second implementation and no radio has read them.
P3-LIMIT-NEAR-SENTENCE: The region in which ranging holds the position budget, two or more beacons in line of sight, covers 23 % of driving steps and was chosen after the results. In the simulation, on assumed ranging errors, the 95th percentile at today's fleet is 24.7 m within a kilometre of the base and 50.1 m under the registered wording, outside the budget in every seed. Inside the narrow region the result rests on the long-range ranging error, an assumption without a lunar measurement: at 10 m in place of 3 m the percentile is 9.6 m. The beacon survey error and the ultra-wideband reach were not swept, and the readings were not computed at eight times the fleet. Inside the region 2.9 % of the steps still exceed the budget.
P3-E53-DESIGN-SENTENCE: E53 computes the traffic of the protocol from the serialised sizes of version 0.1. Each rover sends a position report at 0.1, 1 or 10 Hz whether it moves or not (the protocol's own default is 1 Hz moving and 0.1 Hz parked), status and intent reports at 0.1 Hz, and the market and reservation events at the rates E48 counted at today's fleet. Reports travel one hop; events are relayed to the base. For 5, 10, 20, 40 and 80 rovers, 30 draws place the rovers on the terrain mesh, every one with a 2.5 m antenna although half of today's fleet carries 1.0 m, in two geometries: at positions taken from the recorded trajectories of E50's first seed with every vehicle-step equally likely, which is the registered geometry of H13, and uniformly over all route samples (added after the first results, Section 4.6). In that trace 97.4 % of the vehicle-steps are parked (347,669 against 9,451 driving), so the registered geometry is a fleet standing at its sites. The outcome is the load on the busiest link, the largest sum of what any one node hears, at the 95th percentile over the draws, with authentication on and off, against the 16 kbit/s target of Section 3.4 as load and as airtime at the access efficiencies of E48.
P3-E53-RESULTS-SENTENCE: At the sizes of version 0.1 and with authentication, a rover that reports its position once a second generates 49.1 B/s, 0.393 kbit/s, against 32.3 B/s without it: the security header and the code add 52 % to the bit rate, because they are 14 B on reports of 10 to 15 B of content. For 20 rovers in the fleet geometry the busiest link carries 7.86 kbit/s at 1 Hz with authentication and 5.17 without, and 66.9 and 44.0 kbit/s at 10 Hz; that link carries the sum over the whole fleet, because the fleet works within one radio neighbourhood of the base. As airtime the 1 Hz traffic of 20 rovers needs 9.82 kbit/s of a scheduled channel, within the target, and 21.36 on slotted random access, above it, the same verdicts as E48's event counts gave in Section 5.2. On a scheduled channel the authenticated 1 Hz traffic fits the target for up to 20 rovers of the sizes run and not for 40; at 10 Hz 5 rovers already load the busiest link with 16.7 kbit/s (Table 14).
P3-H13-VERDICT-SENTENCE: H13 of [67] says that with authentication on and 20 rovers the busiest link carries no more than 16 kbit/s at 1 Hz position reports and more at 10 Hz. It is not a test but a design calculation, as a dated entry of [67] records: in the registered geometry every rover is in one radio neighbourhood, so the busiest link carries the fleet's sum in every draw, 20 × 49.1 B/s × 8 = 7.86 kbit/s at 1 Hz and 66.9 kbit/s at 10 Hz, the product of the serialised sizes and the assumed rates that Section 5.2 already gives. It could not have come out otherwise. Its comparison is of load with the target; as airtime, the comparison that change 11 of [59] adopted, the 1 Hz case is above the target on slotted random access (21.36 kbit/s) and within it on a channel the base schedules (9.82 kbit/s).
P3-E53-SPREAD-SENTENCE: With the rovers spread uniformly over the route samples (post hoc) the busiest link at 1 Hz carries 4.54 kbit/s for 20 rovers, 58 % of the fleet geometry's, because each node hears fewer neighbours; the rovers that reach the base need 1.1 to 2.2 hops on average against 1.01 to 1.03; and only 30 %, 43 %, 62 %, 83 % and 93 % of 5, 10, 20, 40 and 80 rovers reach the base at all, against 97 % to 99 % in the fleet geometry.
P3-E53-SPREAD-CLAUSE: E53 measures the other case directly (Section 5.11): with 20 rovers spread uniformly over the route samples the rovers that reach the base need 1.8 hops on average, the busiest link carries 58 % of the load it carries when the fleet works near the base, and only 62 % of the rovers reach the base at all
P3-DTN-MODEL-SENTENCE: In the model of E54 a custodian retransmits after 10 s while the link lasts and holds the bundle, in a store of 64 MB, while there is no path; a vehicle unheard for 10 min retraces its path at half speed to the last point where it had a link; a segment whose holder is still unheard 60 s after the reservation's timeout is marked unconfirmed; and the silent vehicle's task returns to the auction when its 1 h lease expires (Assumed values, [68]). E54 was run with the rule as first written, in which the base released the reservation at that moment; the release is withdrawn, as above, and Section 5.12 reports what E54's counts mean under the rule as it now stands.
P3-E54-DESIGN-SENTENCE: E54 is a simulation at the level of messages over the recorded month of E50, not a new run of the logistics engine: inside the engine a lost message is retried and the regimes know at once that it failed, so a lost job cannot occur there. The contact plan is the terrain mesh along the recorded trajectories, per 60 s step. The traffic is the month's real events: a task award from the base to each job's vehicle, which lives for the 1 h lease, and whose expiry is counted as a lost job (hypothetically: in the recorded run every job was done); a reservation grant, which lives 60 s; a task-state report at the job's end; a daily ledger bundle of 10 kB to Earth with a lifetime of 14 days; and a status report every 10 s, from which the age of the base's information is taken. Earth is blacked out from day 8 to day 22 on top of the month's own direct-to-Earth gaps. Three protocols carry the traffic: drop-and-retry end to end, a try every 180 s and at most five tries, so that it gives up after 12 min on an award that lives an hour (the retry budget is our choice; the registration does not fix it, and it was not swept); store-and-forward hop by hop with custody; and store-and-forward with the lost-link ladder of Section 3.8. The per-hop loss is 0.10, 0.25 or 0.40, on 30 seeds with 199 jobs and 88 single-lane reservations a seed. Two things are approximations: the return of a silent vehicle is applied to the contact plan and is not driven in the engine, and a returning vehicle is given a direct link to the base, which is optimistic when its last link went through another vehicle. E54 also counts the reservations whose holder has no path to the base 60 s after the reservation's timeout: the base cannot confirm that the segment is clear, although in the replay every vehicle left on schedule. Under the rule as it now stands these are the segments marked unconfirmed. The run itself used the rule as first written, which released them and so recorded none by construction; that zero is not a result. The registration also lists the wait of urgent cargo among E54's outcomes; a replay of messages does not move cargo, so that outcome is not reported. The ledger is simulated separately over 61 days, so that every bundle created in the month resolves, with lifetimes of 14 days, 30 days, and the longest Earth outage plus one day.
P3-E54-RESULTS-SENTENCE: At a per-hop loss of 0.25, drop-and-retry lost 10 of 6,028 task awards (4 at a loss of 0.10 and 85 at 0.40), store-and-forward with custody 2 and, with the lost-link rule, 0; the mean delay of an award was 61.5 s, 3.3 s and 3.3 s. Of the reservation grants, which live 60 s and so get one try under drop-and-retry, 1,543 were lost (25.6 %), against 2 and 0; a lost grant is a vehicle that stops before a single-lane segment. Of 6,022 task-state reports, 1,946, 82 and 2 were lost, and custody alone delivered them after 9.0 min on average, the time a report waits in a vehicle that ended its job out of reach, against 33.0 s with the lost-link rule. The base's information about a vehicle was 88.1 min old on average without the rule, and up to 30.9 h for the worst vehicle, with either transport; with the rule it was 45.5 s and 2.5 min. E54 counted 2,566 reservations whose holder had no path to the base 60 s after the reservation's timeout, 7,349 hours in all until the holder was heard, about 98 % of the single-lane reservations, because those segments lie on routes the mast does not see. Under the rule as it now stands these are the segments marked unconfirmed, which another vehicle may enter only at caution speed. The run with the ladder recorded none, because the rule as first written released them at that moment; that zero followed from the rule's definition and is withdrawn as a result, the count with the ladder in force was not recomputed, and the cost of crossing an unconfirmed segment at caution speed is not priced. The ladder sent a silent vehicle back along its path 82.1 times a seed, about 2.6 a day for the eight vehicles; the replay does not drive those returns, each at half speed, and no delay figure contains them (Table 15).
P3-E54-V02-SENTENCE: The replay was repeated at the packet sizes of protocol version 0.2 and with every packet in a Proximity-1 frame, on the same 30 seeds: no value of Table 15 and no verdict changes. That is a property of the replay's message set, not a test of version 0.2. The replay sends task awards, reservation grants and task states, whose sizes version 0.2 does not change (92, 94 and 33 B; 104, 106 and 45 B framed), and in the replay a size counts only against a node's store of 64 MB: with every message of a seed held at once the store would hold 0.37 MB at most. Losses and delays come from the contact plan and the per-hop loss, which do not depend on a message's size.

P3-B97-DESIGN-SENTENCE: Two checks use real data, and each is named for what it is. The first takes six raw frames of the optical-navigation camera of the Artemis II flyby, taken between 2 April 2026 and 10 April 2026 [115], fits a circle to the bright limb of the disc in each (a threshold, a robust circle fit, a least-squares refinement), and turns the disc's radius and centre into a range and a direction with the focal length of the mission's instrument kernel, 7,312 pixels; the truth is the mission's own trajectory and attitude kernels [116]. Nothing is calibrated, and the body in view is taken from the geometry, not from the archive label. This is limb navigation of a crewed spacecraft in cislunar space, 79,000 to 186,000 km from the body in view; it is not surface navigation and not rover data. It tests a camera model, the frames and the kernels of the kind that position-from-image code would rest on; no result of this paper uses such code, because the terrain fix of E50 is a Gaussian draw. The second check compares the Earth-link geometry code of [58], which the Earth windows of this paper come from, with the SPICE toolkit's own routine for azimuth and elevation, for the spacecraft seen from the base at 212 hourly epochs of its trajectory, and measures how far the base moves when the lunar frame kernel is left out (Section 3.7). The spacecraft is below the base's horizon at every one of those epochs (elevation −9.26° to −0.04°), so the check exercises the transformation to azimuth and elevation and not the terrain mask that makes the Earth windows.
P3-B97-RESULTS-SENTENCE: Artemis II optical navigation: of the six frames, one is saturated and five usable; four of those have attitude data and one gives a range only. The range from the fitted disc was 0.25 % to 1.29 % above the kernels' range, and the direction within 0.08° to 0.16°. The errors are not random: the fitted radius was 0.8 to 1.3 pixels small in every frame, which puts every range high, and the angle off the camera's axis was 0.08° to 0.11° low in every frame, which may be the alignment of the camera frame (the mission's frame kernel carries a warning about those angles). We report the bias as it is and do not fit it away; a correction fitted on other frames is the next check. Two of the five discs are Earth, although every archive label names the Moon. For the two frames of the Moon at about 79,000 km the error is 408 to 661 km in range and, at the direction errors above, about 110 to 230 km across the line of sight. That says the geometry chain recovers a real body's range to about a percent and its direction to a tenth or two of a degree from one uncalibrated frame. It says nothing about the 1.7 m of a rover's terrain fix (Table 4): that matches craters metres away against a map, a different measurement at a different scale. Earth-link geometry: over 212 epochs the code's azimuth and elevation agreed with the routine of the toolkit it is built on to 6 × 10<sup>−14</sup>°; without the lunar frame kernel the base moved by 77.4 m, the silent error of Section 3.7 measured at our site.

The sphere's bulge at mid-path, d<sup>2</sup>/8R, is 1.80 m of the rover antennas' 2.5 m at 5 km, and 1.00 m, the antenna height itself, at the 3.73 km horizon of two 1.0 m antennas, where Table 7 evaluates the law for the small classes. A calculation of the loss there with the smooth-sphere method of our own reference [20] (ITU-R P.526, section 3.2, checked against its text) gives 137.0 dB against the 132.0 dB above for the rover antennas, and 146.6 dB against 142.9 dB for the small ones, 4 to 5 dB higher, which puts the flat-ground rates of Table 7 2.2 to 2.4 times too high for the vehicle hops and 1.3 times for the mast (701, 24.6, 48.9 and 3,653 kbit/s in place of 1,574, 57.9, 114 and 4,717 for the crew and cargo rovers, the small rover, the hopper and the mast; Table 7 has both columns). P3-PROP8-EXAMPLE: Worked example, the four beacons of E50 (the base mast, the depot, the power plant and one landing pad): they span 1.37 km and lie nearly on one line. With all four in view the dilution is 8.9 seen from the construction site, 0.26 km from the base; 1.2 seen from the oxygen plant, 1.2 km from the base; 5.2 seen from the science site, 2.1 km from the base; 7.0 seen from the shadowed crater, 4.0 km from the base. It does not simply rise with distance: the site nearest the base is the worst of the four, because it lies almost on the beacons' line (case iii). With the 3 m range error of the base radio the bound on the horizontal error of one epoch (one sigma) is 27 m, 3.7 m, 15 m and 21 m at those four sites. Three things limit what this says about E50. The bound assumes all four beacons in view, while E50's region away from the base is where fewer than two are: it says nothing about the 57 m that E50's ranging layer left there at the 95th percentile. It is a bound for a single epoch of ranges with no prior, while E50 runs a sequential filter with a dead-reckoning prior, which is not bound by it: where two or more beacons are seen E50's median error is 1.1 m, below the single-epoch bound at every one of these sites. P3-P6-ABSTRACT-CLAUSE: Ranging holds the 95th percentile of position error at 4.2 m where two or more base beacons are in line of sight, 23 % of driving steps, and fails under the registered wording, all driving (50.1 m); terrain fixes leave 15.2 m elsewhere. Authentication adds 52 % to the bit rate; senders declare frame, datum and time scale, and reports carry a 95 % bound, not a covariance.
P3-P6-INTRO-CLAUSE: Of the layers under the market, with the hypotheses of [67]: dead reckoning alone passes the 5 m separation budget within the first driving hour (H9′, first clause, supported). Whether ranging holds the budget near the base (second clause) depends on the reading of the registered words: the 95th percentile is 4.22 m where two or more of the four beacons are in line of sight, 23.1 % of driving steps, 24.7 m within a kilometre of the base, and 50.1 m under the registered wording taken literally, where it fails in every seed. Terrain fixes leave 15.2 m elsewhere, and 7.54 m even with a navigation service as assumed for 2030 (third clause, not supported); with the fix stops inside the engine the delay per delivery rises by 0.63 h, 3.5 %, a lower bound from an exploratory run. A crystal oscillator resynchronised whenever the base is heard caused no reservation conflict with a guard of 0.1 s in 303 reservation pairs (H11's first half, observed); that its error exceeds the ranging radio's noise follows from the assumed transfer residual and is a design calculation. Two registered hypotheses are design calculations and are reported as such: by the assumed change rate the changed tiles of a day are 1.06 % of a full resend (H12), and 20 rovers load the busiest link with 7.86 kbit/s at 1 Hz, their sizes times their rates (H13). Authentication adds 52 % to the bit rate of protocol version 0.1. Its position report named neither frame, datum nor time scale; version 0.2 has each sender declare them under its key and puts a 95 % bound in every report, at 8.37 kbit/s for the same 20 rovers, and carries no covariance. Store-and-forward with a lost-link rule lost no job where drop-and-retry lost 0.33 a seed (H14's first clause, supported; 10 awards of 6,028, at a retry budget we chose); its second clause is not testable as written, and the rule now marks a silent holder's segment unconfirmed instead of releasing its reservation. A ledger bundle that lives 14 days does not outlast an Earth outage of 24.8 days, so 11 of the month's 31 daily bundles expire with store-and-forward and none with a lifetime of 25.8 days, a calculation from the calendar.
P3-P6-DISCUSSION-CLAUSE: Where two or more of the four beacons are in line of sight, ranging holds the 95th percentile of the position error at 4.22 m, inside the 5 m budget; that region is 23.1 % of the driving steps, and under wider readings of “near the base” the budget is not held (Section 5.8). In the recorded months a crystal resynchronised at every contact caused no reservation conflict with a guard of 0.1 s; a day of map changes is 1.97 MB at the assumed change rate; and the authenticated reports of 20 rovers would need 9.82 kbit/s of a scheduled channel if every rover were within one hop of the base. Elsewhere, terrain fixes leave the 95th percentile at 15.2 m (7.54 m with a navigation service as assumed for 2030, still outside the budget), a driving vehicle has a radio path to the base in 56.6 % of its steps, and of 20 rovers spread over the routes only 62 % reach the base at all.
P3-P6-CONCLUSION-CLAUSE: Ranging holds the 5 m position budget where two or more beacons are in line of sight (23 % of driving steps), not under wider readings of near the base, and terrain fixes do not hold it elsewhere. Authentication adds 52 % to the bit rate, and senders now declare frame, datum and time scale.
